entries.c25fb198d2501662e71fecde26bc53464b790927: <div sID="gen25298" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Luke.3" sID="Luke.3"/> <div eID="gen25298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25299" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25300" type="x-p"/> Nothing is related concerning our Lord Jesus from his twelfth year to his entrance on his thirtieth year. We often think it would have been a pleasure and advantage to us if we had journals, or at least annuls, of occurrences concerning him; but we have as much as Infinite Wisdom thought fit to communicate to us, and, if we improve not that, neither should we have improved more if we had had it. The great intention of the evangelists was to give us an account of the gospel of Christ, which we are to believe, and by which we hope for salvation: now that began in the ministry and baptism of John, and therefore they hasten to give us an account of that. We could wish, perhaps, that Luke had wholly passed by what was related by Matthew and Mark, and had written only what was new, as he has done in his two first chapters. But it was the will of the Spirit that some things should be established out of the mouth, not only of two, but of three witnesses; and we must not reckon it a needless repetition, nor shall we do so if we renew out meditations upon these things, with suitable affections. In this chapter we have, I. The beginning of John's baptism, and the scope and intention of it, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.1-Luke.3.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. His exhortation to the multitude (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.7-Luke.3.9">ver. 7-9</reference>), and the particular instructions he gave to those who desired to be told their duty, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.10-Luke.3.14">ver. 10-14</reference>. II. The notice he gave them of the approach of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.15-Luke.3.18">ver. 15-18</reference>), to which is added (though it happened after what follows) the mention of his imprisonment, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.19-Luke.3.20">ver. 19-20</reference>. III. Christ coming to be baptized of John, and his entrance therein upon the execution of his prophetical office, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.21-Luke.3.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. IV. His pedigree and genealogy recorded up to Adam, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.23-Luke.3.38">ver. 23-38</reference>.
entries.d9870ea84c53c2c359261d2124ee5583af0fa784: <div eID="gen25300" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25299" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ministry of John the Baptist.</title> <div sID="gen25301" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Cæsar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judæa, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituræa and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene, <hi type="super">2</hi> Annas and Caiaphas being the high priests, the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness. 3 And he came into all the country about Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins; <hi type="super">4</hi> As it is written in the book of the words of Esaias the prophet, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. <hi type="super">5</hi> Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> made smooth; <hi type="super">6</hi> And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. 7 Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <hi type="super">8</hi> Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to <hi type="italic">our</hi> father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. <hi type="super">9</hi> And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: every tree therefore which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the people asked him, saying, What shall we do then? <hi type="super">11</hi> He answereth and saith unto them, He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then came also publicans to be baptized, and said unto him, Master, what shall we do? <hi type="super">13</hi> And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse <hi type="italic">any</hi> falsely; and be content with your wages. <div eID="gen25301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25302" type="x-p"/> John's baptism introducing a new dispensation, it was requisite that we should have a particular account of it. Glorious things were said of John, what a distinguished favourite of Heaven he should be, and what a great blessing to this earth (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.15">ch. i. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">17</reference>); but we lost him in the deserts, and there he remains until <hi type="italic">the day of his showing unto Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.80">ch. i. 80</reference>. And now at last that day dawns, and a welcome day it was to them that waited for it more than they that waited for the morning. Observe here, <div eID="gen25302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25303" type="x-p"/> I. The date of the beginning of John's baptism, when it was that he appeared; this is here taken notice of, which was not by the other evangelists, that the truth of the thing might be confirmed by the exact fixing of the time. And it is dated, <div eID="gen25303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25304" type="x-p"/> 1. By the government of the heathen, which the Jews were under, to show that they were a conquered people, and therefore it was time for the Messiah to come to set up a spiritual kingdom, and an eternal one, upon the ruins of all the temporal dignity and dominion of David and Judah. <div eID="gen25304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25305" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is dated by the reign of the Roman emperor; it was in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Cæsar, the third of the twelve Cæsars, a very bad man, given to covetousness, drunkenness, and cruelty; such a man is mentioned first (saith Dr. Lightfoot), as it were, to teach us what to look for from that cruel and abominable city wherein Satan reigned in all ages and successions. The people of the Jews, after a long struggle, were of late made a province of the empire, and were under the dominion of this Tiberius; and that country which once had made so great a figure, and had many nations tributaries to it, in the reigns of David and Solomon, is now itself an inconsiderable despicable part of the Roman empire, and rather trampled upon than triumphed in. <div eID="gen25305" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen25306"/> <l level="1" sID="gen25307"/><hi type="italic">——En quo discordia cives,</hi><l eID="gen25307" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen25308"/><hi type="italic">Perduxit miseros</hi>——<l eID="gen25308" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen25309"/>What dire effects from civil discord flow!<l eID="gen25309" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen25306"/> <div sID="gen25310" type="x-p"/> The lawgiver was now departed from between Judah's feet; and, as an evidence of that, their public acts are dated by the reign of the Roman emperor, and therefore now Shiloh must come. <div eID="gen25310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25311" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is dated by the governments of the viceroys that ruled in the several parts of the Holy Land under the Roman emperor, which was another badge of their servitude, for they were all foreigners, which bespeaks a sad change with that people whose <hi type="italic">governors</hi> used to be <hi type="italic">of themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>), and it was their glory. <hi type="italic">How is the gold become dim!</hi> [1.] Pilate is here said to be the governor, president, or procurator, of Judea. This character is given of him by some other writers, that he was a wicked man, and one that made no conscience of a lie. He reigned ill, and at last was displaced by Vitellius, president of Syria, and sent to Rome, to answer for his mal-administrations. [2.] The other three are called <hi type="italic">tetrarchs,</hi> some think from the countries which they had the command of, each of them being over a <hi type="italic">fourth part</hi> of that which had been entirely under the government of Herod the Great. Others think that they are so called from the post of honour they held in the government; they had the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> place, or were <hi type="italic">fourth-rate</hi> governors: the emperor was the <hi type="italic">first,</hi> the <hi type="italic">pro-consul,</hi> who governed a province, the <hi type="italic">second,</hi> a <hi type="italic">king</hi> the <hi type="italic">third,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">tetrarch</hi> the <hi type="italic">fourth.</hi> So Dr. Lightfoot. <div eID="gen25311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25312" type="x-p"/> 2. By the government of the Jews among themselves, to show that they were a corrupt people, and that therefore it was time that the Messiah should come, to reform them, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.2">v. 2</reference>. Annas and Caiaphas were the high priests. God had appointed that there should be but one high priest at a time, but here were two, to serve some ill turn or other: one served one year and the other the other year; so some. One was the high priest, and the other the <hi type="italic">sagan,</hi> as the Jews called him, to officiate for him when he was disabled; or, as others say, one was high priest, and represented Aaron, and that was <hi type="italic">Caiaphas;</hi> Annas, the other, was <hi type="italic">nasi,</hi> or head of the sanhedrim, and represented Moses. But to us there is but one high priest, one Lord of all, to whom all judgment is committed. <div eID="gen25312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25313" type="x-p"/> II. The origin and tendency of John's baptism. <div eID="gen25313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25314" type="x-p"/> 1. The origin of it was <hi type="italic">from heaven: The word of God came unto John,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.2">v. 2</reference>. He received full commission and full instructions from God to do what he did. It is the same expression that is used concerning the Old-Testament prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.2">Jer. i. 2</reference>); for John was a prophet, yea, more than a prophet, and in him prophecy revived, which had been long suspended. We are not told how <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord came</hi> to John, whether by an angel, as to his father, or by dream, or vision, or voice, but it was to his satisfaction, and ought to be to ours. John is here called <hi type="italic">the son of Zacharias,</hi> to refer us to what the angel said to his father, when he assured him that he should have this son. The word of the Lord came to him <hi type="italic">in the wilderness;</hi> for those whom God <hi type="italic">fits</hi> he will find out, wherever they are. As the word of the Lord is not <hi type="italic">bound</hi> in a <hi type="italic">prison,</hi> so it is not <hi type="italic">lost</hi> in a <hi type="italic">wilderness.</hi> The <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> made its way to Ezekiel among the captives by the river of Chebar, and to John in the isle of Patmos. John was the <hi type="italic">son of a priest,</hi> now entering upon the thirtieth year of his age; and therefore, according to the custom of the temple, he was now to be admitted into the temple-service, where he should have attended as a candidate five years before. But God had called him to a more honourable ministry, and therefore the Holy Ghost enrols him here, since he was not enrolled in the archives of the temple: <hi type="italic">John the son of Zacharias began his ministration such a time.</hi> <div eID="gen25314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25315" type="x-p"/> 2. The scope and design of it were to bring all the people of his country off from their sins and home to their God, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">He came</hi> first <hi type="italic">into all the country about Jordan,</hi> the neighbourhood wherein he resided, that part of the country which Israel took possession of first, when they entered the land of promise under Joshua's conduct; there was the banner of the gospel first displayed. John resided in the most solitary part of the country: but, when the word of the Lord came to him, he quitted his deserts, and came into the inhabited country. Those that are <hi type="italic">best pleased</hi> in their retirements must cheerfully <hi type="italic">exchange</hi> them, when God calls them into places of concourse. <hi type="italic">He came</hi> out of the wilderness <hi type="italic">into all the country,</hi> with some marks of distinction, <hi type="italic">preaching</hi> a new <hi type="italic">baptism;</hi> not a sect, or party, but a <hi type="italic">profession,</hi> or distinguishing badge. The sign, or ceremony, was such as was ordinarily used among the Jews, <hi type="italic">washing with water,</hi> by which proselytes were sometimes admitted, or disciples to some great master; but the meaning of it was, <hi type="italic">repentance for the remission of sins:</hi> that is, all that submitted to his baptism, <div eID="gen25315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25316" type="x-p"/> (1.) Were thereby obliged to <hi type="italic">repent of their sins,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">sorry</hi> for what they had done amiss, and to <hi type="italic">do so no more.</hi> The former they <hi type="italic">professed,</hi> and were concerned to be <hi type="italic">sincere</hi> in their professions; the latter they <hi type="italic">promised,</hi> and were concerned to <hi type="italic">make good</hi> what they promised. He bound them, not to such ceremonious observances as were imposed by the tradition of the elders, but to change their mind, and change their way, to <hi type="italic">cast away from them all their transgressions,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">make them new hearts</hi> and to live new lives. The design of the gospel, which now began, was to make men devout and pious, holy and heavenly, humble and meek, sober and chaste, just and honest, charitable and kind, and good in every relation, who had been much otherwise; and this is to <hi type="italic">repent.</hi> <div eID="gen25316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25317" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were thereby assured of the pardon of their sins, upon their repentance. As the baptism he administered bound them not to submit to the power of sin, so it sealed to them a gracious and pleadable discharge from the guilt of sin. <hi type="italic">Turn yourselves from all your transgressions, so iniquity shall not be your ruin;</hi> agreeing with the word of the Lord, by the Old-Testament prophets, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.30">Ezek. xviii. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen25317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25318" type="x-p"/> III. The fulfilling of the scriptures in the ministry of John. The other evangelists had referred us to the same text that is here referred to, that of Esaias, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">ch. xl. 3</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">written in the book of the words of Esaias the prophet,</hi> which he heard from God, which he spoke for God, those words of his which were <hi type="italic">written</hi> for the generations to come. Among them it is found that there should be <hi type="italic">the voice of one crying in the wilderness;</hi> and John is that voice, a clear distinct voice, a loud voice, an articulate one; he cries, <hi type="italic">Prepare ye the way of the Lord, and make his paths straight.</hi> John's business is to <hi type="italic">make way</hi> for the entertainment of the gospel in the hearts of the people, to bring them into such a frame and temper as that Christ might be welcome to them, and they welcome to Christ. Luke goes further on with the quotation than Matthew and Mark had done, and applies the following words likewise to John's ministry (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.5-Luke.3.6">v. 5, 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Every valley shall be filled.</hi> Dr. Hammond understands this as a prediction of the desolation coming upon the people of the Jews for their infidelity: the land should be made plain by the pioneers for the Roman army, and should be laid waste by it, and there should then be a visible distinction made between the impenitent on the one side and the receivers of the gospel on the other side. But it seems rather to be meant of the gospel of Christ, of which that was the introduction. 1. The humble shall by it be <hi type="italic">enriched</hi> with grace: <hi type="italic">Every valley</hi> that lies <hi type="italic">low</hi> and <hi type="italic">moist</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">filled</hi> and be <hi type="italic">exalted.</hi> 2. The proud shall by it be humbled; the <hi type="italic">self-confident</hi> that stand upon <hi type="italic">their own bottom,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">self-conceited</hi> that lift up <hi type="italic">their own top,</hi> shall have contempt put upon them: <hi type="italic">Every mountain and hill shall be brought low.</hi> If they repent, they are brought to the dust; if not, to the lowest hell. 3. Sinners shall be converted to God: <hi type="italic">The crooked ways</hi> and the <hi type="italic">crooked</hi> spirits shall be <hi type="italic">made straight;</hi> for, though <hi type="italic">none can make that straight which God hath made crooked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Eccl. vii. 13</reference>), yet God by his grace can make that straight which sin hath made crooked. 4. Difficulties that were hindering and discouraging in the way to heaven shall be removed: <hi type="italic">The rough ways shall be made smooth;</hi> and they that love God's law shall have <hi type="italic">great peace,</hi> and <hi type="italic">nothing shall offend them.</hi> The gospel has made the way to heaven <hi type="italic">plain</hi> and easy to be <hi type="italic">found, smooth</hi> and easy to be <hi type="italic">walked in.</hi> 5. The great salvation shall be more fully discovered than ever, and the discovery of it shall spread further (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">All flesh shall see the salvation of God;</hi> not the Jews only, but the Gentiles. All shall <hi type="italic">see</hi> it; they shall have it set before them and offered to them, and some of all sorts shall <hi type="italic">see</hi> it, enjoy it, and have the benefit of it. When way is made for the gospel into the heart, by the captivation of high thoughts and bringing them into obedience to Christ, by the leveling of the soul and the removing of all obstructions that stand in the way of Christ and his grace, then prepare to bid the salvation of God welcome. <div eID="gen25318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25319" type="x-p"/> IV. The general warnings and exhortations which he gave to those who submitted to his baptism, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.7-Luke.3.9">v. 7-9</reference>. In Matthew he is said to have preached these same things to <hi type="italic">many of the Pharisees and Sadducees,</hi> that <hi type="italic">came to his baptism</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.7-Matt.3.10">Matt. iii. 7-10</reference>); but here he is said to have spoken them <hi type="italic">to the multitude, that came forth to be baptized of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.7">v. 7</reference>. This was the purport of his preaching to all that came to him, and he did not alter it in compliment to the Pharisees and Sadducees, when they came, but dealt as plainly with them as with any other of his hearers. And as he did not flatter the <hi type="italic">great,</hi> so neither did he compliment the <hi type="italic">many,</hi> or make his court to them, but gave the same reproofs of sin and warnings of wrath to the <hi type="italic">multitude</hi> that he did to the Sadducees and Pharisees; for, if they had not the same faults, they had others as bad. Now observe here, <div eID="gen25319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25320" type="x-p"/> 1. That the guilty corrupted race of mankind is become a <hi type="italic">generation of vipers;</hi> not only poisoned, but poisonous; hateful to God, hating one another. This magnifies the patience of God, in continuing the race of mankind upon the earth, and not destroying that <hi type="italic">nest of vipers.</hi> He did it once by water, and will again by fire. <div eID="gen25320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25321" type="x-p"/> 2. This generation of vipers is fairly warned to <hi type="italic">flee from the wrath to come,</hi> which is certainly before them if they continue such; and their being a <hi type="italic">multitude</hi> will not be at all their security, for it will be neither <hi type="italic">reproach</hi> nor <hi type="italic">loss</hi> to God to cut them off. We are not only warned of this wrath, but are put into a way to escape it, if we look about us in time. <div eID="gen25321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25322" type="x-p"/> 3. There is no way of <hi type="italic">fleeing from the wrath to come,</hi> but by <hi type="italic">repentance.</hi> They that submitted to the baptism of repentance thereby evidenced that they were <hi type="italic">warned</hi> to flee from the wrath to come and <hi type="italic">took</hi> the warning; and we by our baptism profess to have fled out of Sodom, for fear of what is coming upon it. <div eID="gen25322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25323" type="x-p"/> 4. Those that profess repentance are highly concerned to live like penitents (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance,</hi> else, notwithstanding your professions of repentance, you cannot escape <hi type="italic">the wrath to come.</hi>" By the fruits of repentance it will be known whether it be sincere or no. By the change of our way must be evidenced the change of our mind. <div eID="gen25323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25324" type="x-p"/> 5. If we be not really holy, both in heart and life, our profession of religion and relation to God and his church will stand us in no stead at all: <hi type="italic">Begin not</hi> now to frame excuses from this great duty of repentance, by <hi type="italic">saying within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father.</hi> What will it avail us to be the children of godly parents if we be not godly, to be within the pale of the Church if we be not brought into the bond of the covenant? <div eID="gen25324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25325" type="x-p"/> 6. We have therefore no reason to depend upon our external privileges and professions of religion, because God has no need of us or of our services, but can effectually secure by his own honour and interest without us. If we were cut off and ruined, he could raise up to himself a church out of the most unlikely,—<hi type="italic">children to Abraham</hi> even <hi type="italic">out of stones.</hi> <div eID="gen25325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25326" type="x-p"/> 7. The greater professions we make of repentance, and the greater assistances and encouragements are given us to repentance, the nearer and the sorer will our destruction be if we do not <hi type="italic">bring forth fruits meet for repentance.</hi> Now that the gospel begins to be preached, now that the kingdom of heaven is at hand, <hi type="italic">now</hi> that the <hi type="italic">axe is laid to the root of the tree,</hi> threatenings to the wicked and impenitent are now more terrible than before, as encouragements to the penitent are now more comfortable. "Now that you are upon your behaviour, look to yourselves." <div eID="gen25326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25327" type="x-p"/> 8. Barren trees will be cast into the fire at length; it is the fittest place for them: <hi type="italic">Every tree</hi> that doth not bring forth fruit, <hi type="italic">good fruit,</hi> is <hi type="italic">hewn down,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cast into the fire.</hi> If it serve not for fruit, to the honour of God's grace, let it serve for fuel, to the honour of his justice. <div eID="gen25327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25328" type="x-p"/> V. The particular instructions he gave to several sorts of persons, that enquired of him concerning their duty: the <hi type="italic">people,</hi> the <hi type="italic">publicans,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">soldiers.</hi> Some of the Pharisees and Sadducees came to his baptism; but we do not find them asking, <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> They thought they knew what they had to do as well as he could tell them, or were determined to do what they pleased, whatever he told them. But the <hi type="italic">people,</hi> the <hi type="italic">publicans,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">soldiers,</hi> who knew that they had done amiss, and that they ought to do better, and were conscious to themselves of great ignorance and unacquaintedness with the divine law, were particularly inquisitive: <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> Note, 1. Those that are <hi type="italic">baptized</hi> must be <hi type="italic">taught,</hi> and those that have baptized them are concerned, as they have opportunity, to teach them, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.19-Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 19, 20</reference>. 2. Those that profess and promise repentance in general must evidence it by particular instances of reformation, according as their place and condition are. 3. They that would do their duty must desire to know their duty, and enquire concerning it. The first good word Paul said, when he was converted, was, <hi type="italic">Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?</hi> These here enquire, not, <hi type="italic">What shall this man do?</hi> but, What shall <hi type="italic">we</hi> do? What <hi type="italic">fruits meet for repentance</hi> shall we <hi type="italic">bring forth?</hi> Now John gives answer to each, according to their place and station. <div eID="gen25328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25329" type="x-p"/> (1.) He tells the <hi type="italic">people</hi> their duty, and that is to be charitable (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.11">v. 11</reference>): He <hi type="italic">that has two coats,</hi> and, consequently, one to spare, let him <hi type="italic">give,</hi> or <hi type="italic">lend</hi> at least, <hi type="italic">to him that has none,</hi> to keep him warm. Perhaps he saw among his hearers some that were overloaded with clothes, while others were ready to perish in rags, and he puts those who had superfluities upon contributing to the relief of those that had not necessaries. The gospel requires <hi type="italic">mercy,</hi> and not sacrifice; and the design of it is to engage us to do all the good we can. <hi type="italic">Food and raiment</hi> are the two supports of life; he that hath <hi type="italic">meat</hi> to spare, let him give to him that is destitute of <hi type="italic">daily food,</hi> as well as he that hath clothes to spare: what we have we are but stewards of, and must use it, accordingly, as our Master directs. <div eID="gen25329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25330" type="x-p"/> (2.) He tells the <hi type="italic">publicans</hi> their duty, the collectors of the emperor's revenue (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Exact no more than that which is appointed you.</hi> They must do justice between the government and the merchant, and not oppress the people in levying the taxes, nor any way make them heavier or more burdensome than the law had made them. They must not think that because it was their office to take care that the people did not defraud the prince they might therefore, by the power they had, bear hard upon the people; as those that have ever so little a branch of power are apt to abuse it: "No, keep to your <hi type="italic">book of rates,</hi> and reckon it enough that you collect for Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's, and do not enrich yourselves by taking more." The public revenues must be applied to the public service, and not to gratify the avarice of private persons. Observe, He does not direct the publicans to quit their places, and to go no more to the receipt of custom; the employment is in itself lawful and necessary, but let them be just and honest in it. <div eID="gen25330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25331" type="x-p"/> (3.) He tells the <hi type="italic">soldiers</hi> their duty, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.14">v. 14</reference>. Some think that these soldiers were of the Jewish nation and religion: others think that they were Romans; for it was not likely either that the Jews would serve the Romans or that the Romans would trust the Jews in their garrisons in their own nation; and then it is an early instance of Gentiles embracing the gospel and submitting to it. Military men seldom seem inclined to religion; yet these submitted even to the Baptist's strict profession, and desired to receive the <hi type="italic">word of command</hi> from him: <hi type="italic">What must we do?</hi> Those who more than other men have their lives in their hands, and are in deaths often, are concerned to enquire what they shall do that they may be <hi type="italic">found in peace.</hi> In answer to this enquiry, John does not bid them lay down their arms, and desert the service, but cautions them against the sins that soldiers were commonly guilty of; for this is fruit meet for repentance, to <hi type="italic">keep ourselves from our iniquity.</hi> [1.] They must not be injurious to <hi type="italic">the people</hi> among whom they were quartered, and over whom indeed they were set: "<hi type="italic">Do violence to no man.</hi> Your business is to keep the peace, and prevent men's doing violence to one another; but do not you <hi type="italic">do violence</hi> to any. <hi type="italic">Shake no man</hi>" (so the word signifies); "do not put people into fear; for the sword of war, as well as that of justice, is to be a terror only to evil doers, but a protection to those that do well. Be not rude in your quarters; force not money from people by frightening them. Shed not the blood of war in peace; offer no incivility either to man or woman, nor have any hand in the barbarous devastations that armies sometimes make." Nor must they <hi type="italic">accuse any falsely</hi> to the government, thereby to make themselves formidable, and get bribes. [2.] They must not be injurious to their <hi type="italic">fellow-soldiers;</hi> for some think that caution, not to <hi type="italic">accuse falsely,</hi> has special reference to them: "Be not forward to complain one of another to your superior officers, that you may be revenged on those whom you have a pique against, or undermine those above you, and get into their places." <hi type="italic">Do not oppress any;</hi> so some think the word here signifies as used by the LXX. in several passages of the Old Testament. [3.] They must not be given to mutiny, or contend with their generals about their pay: "<hi type="italic">Be content with your wages.</hi> While you have what you agreed for, do not murmur that it is not more." It is discontent with what they have that makes men oppressive and injurious; they that never think they have enough themselves will not scruple at any the most irregular practices to make it more, by defrauding others. It is a rule to all servants that they <hi type="italic">be content with their wages;</hi> for they that indulge themselves in discontents expose themselves to many temptations, and it is wisdom to make the best of that which is.
entries.eaf2c9a959985e0d4dc253cf886f50b2e9b5a25a: <div eID="gen25331" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Imprisonment of John the Baptist.</title> <div sID="gen25332" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And as the people were in expectation, and all men mused in their hearts of John, whether he were the Christ, or not; <hi type="super">16</hi> John answered, saying unto <hi type="italic">them</hi> all, I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire: <hi type="super">17</hi> Whose fan <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his hand, and he will thoroughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable. <hi type="super">18</hi> And many other things in his exhortation preached he unto the people. <hi type="super">19</hi> But Herod the tetrarch, being reproved by him for Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and for all the evils which Herod had done, <hi type="super">20</hi> Added yet this above all, that he shut up John in prison. <div eID="gen25332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25333" type="x-p"/> We are now drawing near to the appearance of our Lord Jesus publicly; the Sun will not be long after the morning-star. We are here told, <div eID="gen25333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25334" type="x-p"/> I. How the people took occasion, from the ministry and baptism of John, to think of the Messiah, and to think of him as at the door, as now come. Thus the way of the Lord was <hi type="italic">prepared,</hi> and people were prepared to bid Christ welcome; for, when men's expectations are raised, that which they are in expectation of becomes doubly acceptable. Now when they observed what an excellent doctrine John Baptist preached, what a divine power went along with it, and what a tendency it had to reform the world, 1. They began presently to consider that now was the time for the Messiah to appear. The sceptre was departed from Judah, for they had no king but Cæsar; nay, and the law-giver too was gone from between his feet, for Herod had lately slain the sanhedrim. Daniel's seventy weeks were now expiring; and therefore it was but three or four years after this that they looked that the kingdom of heaven should appear immediately, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.11">Luke xix. 11</reference>. Never did the corrupt state of the Jews more need a reformation, nor their distressed state more need a deliverance, than now. 2. Their next thought was, "Is not his he that should come?" <hi type="italic">All</hi> thinking <hi type="italic">men mused,</hi> or reasoned, <hi type="italic">in their hearts,</hi> concerning John, <hi type="italic">whether he were the Christ or not.</hi> He had indeed none of the external pomp and grandeur in which they generally expected the Messiah to appear; but his life was holy and strict, his preaching powerful and with authority, and therefore "why may we not think that he is the Messiah, and that he will shortly throw off this disguise, and appear in more glory?" Note, That which puts people upon considering, reasoning with themselves, prepares the way for Christ. <div eID="gen25334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25335" type="x-p"/> II. How John disowned all pretensions to the honour of being himself the Messiah, but confirmed them in their expectations of him that really was the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.16-Luke.3.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. John's office, as a crier or herald, was to give notice that the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God</hi> and the King of that kingdom were <hi type="italic">at hand;</hi> and therefore, when he had told all manner of people severally what they must do ("You must do this, and you must do that"), he tells them one thing more which they must all do: they must expect the Messiah now shortly to appear. And this serves as an <hi type="italic">answer</hi> to their <hi type="italic">musings</hi> and debates concerning himself. Though he knew not their thoughts, yet, in declaring this, he <hi type="italic">answered</hi> them. <div eID="gen25335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25336" type="x-p"/> 1. He declares that the utmost he could do was to <hi type="italic">baptize</hi> them <hi type="italic">with water.</hi> He had no access to <hi type="italic">the Spirit,</hi> nor could command <hi type="italic">that</hi> or work upon <hi type="italic">that;</hi> he could only exhort them to <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> and assure them of forgiveness, upon repentance; he could not work repentance in them, nor confer remission on them. <div eID="gen25336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25337" type="x-p"/> 2. He consigns them, and turns them over, as it were, to Jesus Christ, for whom he was sent to <hi type="italic">prepare the way,</hi> and to whom he was ready to transfer all the interest he had in the affections of the people, and would have them no longer to <hi type="italic">debate</hi> whether John was the Messiah or no, but to look for him that was really so. <div eID="gen25337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25338" type="x-p"/> (1.) John owns the Messiah to have a greater <hi type="italic">excellency</hi> than he had, and that he was in all things preferable to him; he is one the <hi type="italic">latchet of whose shoe</hi> he does not think himself <hi type="italic">worthy to loose;</hi> he does not think himself worthy to be the meanest of his servants, to help him on and off with his shoes. John was <hi type="italic">a prophet,</hi> yea <hi type="italic">more than a prophet,</hi> more so than any of the Old-Testament prophets; but Christ was a prophet more than John, for it was both <hi type="italic">by the Spirit of Christ,</hi> and <hi type="italic">of the grace of Christ,</hi> that all the prophets prophesied, and John among the rest, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10-1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 10, 11</reference>. This was a great truth which John came to preach; but the manner of his expressing it bespeaks his humility, and in it he not only <hi type="italic">does justice</hi> to the Lord Jesus, but <hi type="italic">does him honour</hi> too: "He is one whom I am not worthy to approach, or draw nigh to, no not as a servant." Thus highly does it become us to speak of Christ, and thus humbly of ourselves. <div eID="gen25338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25339" type="x-p"/> (2.) He owns him to have a greater <hi type="italic">energy</hi> than he had: "He is <hi type="italic">mightier than I,</hi> and does that which I cannot do, both for the comfort of the faithful and for the terror of hypocrites and dissemblers." They thought that a wonderful power went along with John; but what was that compared with the power which Jesus would come clothed with? [1.] John can do no more than <hi type="italic">baptize with water,</hi> in token of this, that they ought to purify and cleanse themselves; but Christ can, and will, <hi type="italic">baptize with the Holy Ghost;</hi> he can give the Spirit to cleanse and purify the heart, not only as <hi type="italic">water</hi> washes off the <hi type="italic">dirt</hi> on the outside, but as <hi type="italic">fire</hi> purges out the <hi type="italic">dross</hi> that is within, and <hi type="italic">melts down</hi> the metal, that it may be cast into a <hi type="italic">new mould.</hi> [2.] John can only preach a <hi type="italic">distinguishing</hi> doctrine, and by word and sign <hi type="italic">separate between the precious and the vile;</hi> but Christ hath his <hi type="italic">fan in his hand,</hi> with which he can, and will, perfectly separate between the wheat and the chaff. He <hi type="italic">will thoroughly purge his floor;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">his own,</hi> and therefore he will <hi type="italic">purge</hi> it, and will cast out of his church the unbelieving impenitent Jews, and confirm in his church all that faithfully follow him. [3.] John can only <hi type="italic">speak comfort</hi> to those that receive the gospel, and, like other prophets, <hi type="italic">say to the righteous</hi> that <hi type="italic">it shall be well with them;</hi> but Jesus Christ will <hi type="italic">give them comfort.</hi> John can only promise them that they shall be safe; but Christ will make them so: he will <hi type="italic">gather the wheat into his garner;</hi> good, serious, solid people he will gather now into his church on earth, which shall be made up of such, and he will shortly gather them into his church in heaven, where they shall be for ever sheltered. [4.] John can only <hi type="italic">threaten</hi> hypocrites, and tell the <hi type="italic">barren trees</hi> that they shall be <hi type="italic">hewn down</hi> and <hi type="italic">cast into the fire;</hi> but Christ can execute that threatening; those that are as <hi type="italic">chaff,</hi> light, and vain, and worthless, <hi type="italic">he will burn with fire unquenchable.</hi> John refers here to <reference osisRef="Mal.3.18">Mal. iii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1-Mal.4.2">iv. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when the <hi type="italic">floor is purged, ye shall return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the day comes that shall burn as an oven.</hi> <div eID="gen25339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25340" type="x-p"/> The evangelist concludes his account of John's preaching with an <hi type="italic">et cætera</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many other things in his exhortation preached he unto the people,</hi> which are not recorded. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> John was an <hi type="italic">affectionate</hi> preacher. He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parakalon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">exhorting,</hi> beseeching; he pressed things home upon his hearers, followed his doctrine close, as one in earnest. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He was a <hi type="italic">practical</hi> preacher. Much of his preaching was <hi type="italic">exhortation,</hi> quickening them to their duty, directing them in it, and not amusing them with matters of nice speculation. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He was a <hi type="italic">popular</hi> preacher. Though he had scribes and Pharisees, men of polite learning, attending his ministry, and Sadducees, men of <hi type="italic">free thought,</hi> as they pretended, yet he addressed himself <hi type="italic">to the people,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pros ton laon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to the laity,</hi> and accommodated himself to their capacity, as promising himself best success among them. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He was an <hi type="italic">evangelical</hi> preacher, for so the word here used signifies, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">euengelizeto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he preached the gospel</hi> to the people; in all his <hi type="italic">exhortations,</hi> he directed people to Christ, and excited and encouraged their expectations of <hi type="italic">him.</hi> When we press duty upon people, we must direct them to Christ, both for righteousness and strength. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> He was a <hi type="italic">copious</hi> preacher: <hi type="italic">Many other things he preached,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">polla men kai hetera</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">many things, and different.</hi> He preached a great deal, shunned not to declare the whole counsel of God; and he <hi type="italic">varied</hi> in his preaching, that those who were not reached, and touched, and wrought upon, by one truth, might be by another. <div eID="gen25340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25341" type="x-p"/> III. How full a stop was put to John's preaching. When he was in the midst of his usefulness, going on thus successfully, he was imprisoned by the malice of Herod (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.19-Luke.3.20">v. 19, 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Herod the tetrarch being reproved by him,</hi> not only for living in incest with his brother Philip's wife, but for the many other <hi type="italic">evils which Herod had done</hi> (for those that are wicked in one instance are commonly so in many others), he could not <hi type="italic">bear it,</hi> but contracted an antipathy to him for his plain dealing, and <hi type="italic">added</hi> this wickedness to all the rest, which was indeed <hi type="italic">above all,</hi> that he <hi type="italic">shut up John in prison,</hi> put that burning and shining light under a bushel. Because he could not bear his reproofs, others should be deprived of the benefit of his instructions and counsels. Some little good he might do to those who had access to him, when he was in prison; but nothing to what he might have done if he had had liberty to go about all the country, as he had done. We cannot think of Herod's doing this without the greatest compassion and lamentation, nor of God's permitting it without admiring the depth of the divine counsels, which we cannot account for. Must he be silenced who is the <hi type="italic">voice of one crying in the wilderness?</hi> Must such a preacher be shut up in prison who ought to have been set up in the courts of the temple? But thus the faith of his disciples must be tried; thus the unbelief of those who rejected him must be punished; thus he must be Christ's forerunner in suffering as well as preaching; and thus, having been for about a year and a half preparing people for Christ, he must now give way to him, and, the Sun being risen, the morning-star must of course disappear.

type="italic">the son</hi> of Adam, which was <hi type="italic">the son</hi> of God. <div eID="gen25342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25343" type="x-p"/> The evangelist mentioned John's imprisonment before Christ's being baptized, though it was nearly a year after it, because he would finish the story of John's ministry, and then introduce that of Christ. Now here we have, <div eID="gen25343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25344" type="x-p"/> I. A short account of Christ's baptism, which had been more fully related by St. Matthew. Jesus came, to be baptized of John, and he was so, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.21-Luke.3.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. <div eID="gen25344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25345" type="x-p"/> 1. It is here said that, <hi type="italic">when all the people were baptized,</hi> then <hi type="italic">Jesus was baptized:</hi> all that were then present. Christ would be baptized last, among the common people, and in the rear of them; thus he humbled himself, and made himself of no reputation, as one of the least, nay, as less than the least. He saw what multitudes were hereby prepared to receive him, and then he appeared. <div eID="gen25345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25346" type="x-p"/> 2. Notice is here taken of Christ's <hi type="italic">praying</hi> when he was <hi type="italic">baptized,</hi> which was not in Matthew: being baptized, and <hi type="italic">praying.</hi> He did not <hi type="italic">confess sin,</hi> as others did, for he had none to confess; but he <hi type="italic">prayed,</hi> as others did, for he would thus keep up communion with his Father. Note, The inward and spiritual grace of which sacraments are the outward and visible signs must be fetched in by prayer; and therefore prayer must always accompany them. We have reason to think that Christ now prayed for this manifestation of God's favour to him which immediately followed; he prayed for the discovery of his Father's favour to him, and the descent of the Spirit. What was promised to Christ, he must obtain by prayer: <hi type="italic">Ask of me and I will give thee, &c.</hi> Thus he would put an honour upon prayer, would tie us to it, and encourage us in it. <div eID="gen25346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25347" type="x-p"/> 3. When he prayed, <hi type="italic">the heaven was opened.</hi> He that by his power parted the waters, to make a way through them to Canaan, now by his power parted the air, another fluid element, to open a correspondence with the heavenly Canaan. Thus was there opened to Christ, and by him to us, <hi type="italic">a new and living way into the holiest;</hi> sin had shut up heaven, but Christ's prayer opened it again. Prayer is an ordinance that <hi type="italic">opens heaven: Knock, and it shall be opened unto you.</hi> <div eID="gen25347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25348" type="x-p"/> 4. <hi type="italic">The Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him;</hi> our Lord Jesus was now to receive greater measures of the Spirit than before, to qualify him for his prophetical office, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. When he begins to preach, <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord is upon him.</hi> Now this is here expressed by a sensible evidence for his encouragement in his work, and for the satisfaction of John the Baptist; for he was told before that by this sign it should be notified to him which was the Christ. Dr. Lightfoot suggests that the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape, that he might be revealed to be a personal substance, and not merely an operation of the Godhead: and thus (saith he) was made a full, clear, and sensible demonstration of the Trinity, at the beginning of the gospel; and very fitly is this done at Christ's baptism, who was to make the ordinance of baptism a badge of the profession of that faith in the doctrine of the Trinity, <hi type="italic">Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.</hi> <div eID="gen25348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25349" type="x-p"/> 5. There came <hi type="italic">a voice from heaven,</hi> from God the Father, from the <hi type="italic">excellent glory</hi> (so it is expressed, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.17">2 Pet. i. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou art my beloved Son.</hi> Here, and in Mark, it is expressed as spoken <hi type="italic">to</hi> Christ; in Matthew as spoken <hi type="italic">of</hi> him: <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> It comes all to one; it was intended to be a notification to John, and as such was properly expressed by, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son;</hi> and likewise an answer to his prayer, and so it is most fitly expressed by. <hi type="italic">Thou art.</hi> It was foretold concerning the Messiah, <hi type="italic">I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2 Sam. vii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will make him my First-born,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">Ps. lxxxix. 27</reference>. It was also foretold that he should be God's <hi type="italic">elect, in whom his soul delighted</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>); and, accordingly, it is here declared, <hi type="italic">Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.</hi> <div eID="gen25349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25350" type="x-p"/> II. A long account of Christ's pedigree, which had been more briefly related by St. Matthew. Here is, <div eID="gen25350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25351" type="x-p"/> 1. His age: <hi type="italic">He now began to be about thirty years of age.</hi> So old Joseph was when he stood before Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.46">Gen. xli. 46</reference>), David when he began to reign (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.4">2 Sam. v. 4</reference>), and at this age the priests were to enter upon the full execution of their office, <reference osisRef="Num.4.3">Num. iv. 3</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot thinks that it is plain, by the manner of expression here, that he was just twenty-nine years old complete, and entering upon his thirtieth year, in the month <hi type="italic">Tisri;</hi> that, after this, he lived three years and a half, and died when he was thirty-two years and a half old. <hi type="italic">Three years and a half,</hi> the time of Christ's ministry, is a period of time very remarkable in scripture. <hi type="italic">Three years and six months</hi> the heavens were shut up in Elijah's time, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.25">Luke iv. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">Jam. v. 17</reference>. This was the half week in which the Messiah was to confirm the covenant, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan. ix. 27</reference>. This period is expressed in the prophetical writings by a time, times, and half a time (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Dan. xii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.14">Rev. xii. 14</reference>); and by forty-two months, and a thousand two hundred and threescore days, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.2-Rev.11.3">Rev. xi. 2, 3</reference>. It is the time fixed for the witnesses' prophesying in sackcloth, in conformity to Christ's preaching in his humiliation just so long. <div eID="gen25351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25352" type="x-p"/> 2. His pedigree, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.23">v. 23</reference>, &c. Matthew had given us somewhat of this. He goes no higher than Abraham, but Luke brings it as high as Adam. Matthew designed to show that Christ was the son of Abraham, in whom <hi type="italic">all the families of the earth are blessed,</hi> and that he was heir to the throne of David; and therefore he begins with Abraham, and brings the genealogy down to Jacob, who was the father of Joseph, and heir-male of the house of David: but Luke, designing to show that Christ was the <hi type="italic">seed of the woman,</hi> that should break the serpent's head, traces his pedigree upward as high as Adam, and begins it with Ei, or Heli, who was the father, not of Joseph, but of the virgin Mary. And some suggest that the supply which our translators all along insert here is not right, and that it should not be read <hi type="italic">which,</hi> that is, which <hi type="italic">Joseph</hi> was the son of Heli, but which <hi type="italic">Jesus;</hi> he was <hi type="italic">the son of Joseph, of Eli, of Matthat,</hi> &c., and he, that is, Jesus, was the son <hi type="italic">of Seth, of Adam, of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.38">v. 38</reference>. The difference between the two evangelists in the genealogy of Christ has been a stumbling-block to infidels that cavil at the word, but such a one as has been removed by the labours of learned men, both in the early ages of the church and in latter times, to which we refer ourselves. Matthew draws the pedigree from Solomon, whose natural line ending in Jechonias, the legal right was transferred to Salathiel, who was of the house of Nathan, another son of David, which line Luke here pursues, and so leaves out all the kings of Judah. It is well for us that our salvation doth not depend upon our being able to solve all these difficulties, nor is the divine authority of the gospels at all weakened by them; for the evangelists are not supposed to write these genealogies either of their own knowledge or by divine inspiration, but to have copied them out of the authentic records of the genealogies among the Jews, the heralds' books, which therefore they were obliged to follow; and in them they found the pedigree of Jacob, the father of Joseph, to be as it is set down in Matthew; and the pedigree of Heli, the father of Mary, to be as it is set down here in Luke. And this is the meaning of <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hos enomizeto</hi></hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.23">v. 23</reference>), not, <hi type="italic">as it was supposed,</hi> referring only to Joseph, but <hi type="italic">uti sancitum est lege—as it is entered into the books,</hi> as we find it upon record; by which is appeared that Jesus was both by father and mother's side the Son of David, witness this extract out of their own records, which any one might at that time have liberty to compare with the original, and further the evangelists needed not to go; nay, had they varied from that, they had not gained their point. Its not being contradicted at that time is satisfaction enough to us now that it is a true copy, as it is further worthy of observation, that, when those records of the Jewish genealogies had continued thirty or forty years after these extracts out of them, long enough to justify the evangelists therein, they were all lost and destroyed with the Jewish state and nation; for now there was no more occasion for them. <div eID="gen25352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25353" type="x-p"/> One difficulty occurs between Abraham and Noah, which gives us some perplexity, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.35-Luke.3.36">v. 35, 36</reference>. Sala is said to be the <hi type="italic">son of Cainan,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">the son of Arphaxad,</hi> whereas Sala was the son of Arphaxad (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.24">Gen. x. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.11.12">xi. 12</reference>), and there is no such man as Cainan found there. But, as to that, it is sufficient to say that the Seventy Interpreters, who, before our Saviour's time, translated the Old Testament into Greek, for reasons best known to themselves inserted that Cainan; and St. Luke, writing among the <hi type="italic">Hellenist Jews,</hi> was obliged to make use of that translation, and therefore to take it as he found it. <div eID="gen25353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25354" type="x-p"/> The genealogy concludes with this, <hi type="italic">who was the son of Adam, the son of God.</hi> (1.) Some refer it to Adam; he was in a peculiar manner the <hi type="italic">son of God,</hi> being, more immediately than any of his offspring, the offspring of God by creation. (2.) Others refer it to Christ, and so make the last words of this genealogy to denote his divine and human nature. He was both the <hi type="italic">Son of Adam</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> that he might be a proper Mediator between God and the sons of Adam, and might bring the sons of Adam to be, through him, the <hi type="italic">sons of God.</hi>  <chapter eID="Luke.3"/> <div eID="gen25354" type="x-p"/>

entries.3997e638c766cd486460487d8665fb35e0369d6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14306"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.3.1-Luke.3.20">Lu 3:1-20</reference>. Preaching, Baptism, and Imprisonment of John.</title> <div sID="gen27719" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.1-Matt.3.12">Mt 3:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.17">Mr 6:17</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen27719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14306"/>1-2. Here the curtain of the New Testament is, as it were, drawn up, and the greatest of all epochs of the Church commences. Even our Lord's own age (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.23">Lu 3:23</reference>) is determined by it [Bengel]. No such elaborate chronological precision is to be found elsewhere in the New Testament, and it comes fitly from him who claims it as the peculiar recommendation of his Gospel, that he had "accurately traced down all things from the first" (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.3">Lu 1:3</reference>). Here, evidently, commences his proper narrative. Also see on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Mt 3:1</reference>.<div eID="gen27720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fifteenth year of Tiberius--</hi>reckoning from the period when he was admitted, three years before Augustus' death, to a share of the empire [Webster and Wilkinson], about the end of the year of Rome 779, or about four years before the usual reckoning.<div eID="gen27721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pilate ... governor of Judea--</hi>His proper title was Procurator, but with more than the usual powers of that office. After holding it about ten years he was ordered to Rome, to answer to charges brought against him, but ere he arrived Tiberius died (A.D. 35), and soon after Pilate committed suicide.<div eID="gen27722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Herod--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14">Mr 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen27723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Philip--</hi>a different and very superior Philip to the one whose wife Herodias went to live with Herod Antipas. (See <reference osisRef="Mark.6.17">Mr 6:17</reference>).<div eID="gen27724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Iturea--</hi>to the northeast of Palestine; so called from Ishmael's son Itur or Jetur (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.31">1Ch 1:31</reference>), and anciently belonging to the half tribe of Manasseh.<div eID="gen27725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Trachonitis--</hi>farther to the northeast, between Iturea and Damascus; a rocky district, infested by robbers, and committed by Augustus to Herod the Great to keep in order.<div eID="gen27726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Abilene--</hi>still more to the northeast, so called from Abila, eighteen miles from Damascus [Robinson]. <div eID="gen27727" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f6b77ed828ca9941d1424ba2acaa66273dd48e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14318"/><div sID="gen27744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14318"/><hi type="bold">19-20. But Herod, &c.--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14">Mr 6:14</reference>, &c. (Also see on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen27744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and for all the evils which Herod had done--</hi>important fact here only mentioned, showing how thoroughgoing was the fidelity of the Baptist to his royal hearer, and how strong must have been the workings of conscience in that slave of passion when, notwithstanding such plainness, he "did many things and heard John gladly" (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.20">Mr 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.26">26</reference>). <div eID="gen27745" type="x-p"/>
entries.d514fe8fe10e6e1a6b01fd142348fc4b5c4cb1fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14320"/><div sID="gen27749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14320"/><hi type="bold">21. when all the people were baptized--</hi>that He might not seem to be merely one of the crowd. Thus, as He rode into Jerusalem upon an ass, "whereon yet never man sat" (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.30">Lu 19:30</reference>), and lay in a sepulchre "wherein was never man yet laid" (<reference osisRef="John.19.41">Joh 19:41</reference>), so in His baptism He would be "separate from sinners." <div eID="gen27749" type="x-p"/>
entries.21358503bab8d1333793b1f8fb86dffdf87396da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14321"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.3.23-Luke.3.38">Lu 3:23-38</reference>. Genealogy of Jesus.</title> <div sID="gen27750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14321"/><hi type="bold">23. he began to be about thirty--</hi>that is, "was about entering on His thirtieth year." So our translators have taken the word (and so Calvin, Beza, Bloomfield, Webster and Wilkinson, &c.): but "was about thirty years of age when He began [His ministry]," makes better Greek, and is probably the true sense [Bengel, Olshausen, De Wette, Meyer, Alford, &c.]. At this age the priests entered on their office (<reference osisRef="Num.4.3">Nu 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen27750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, &c.--</hi>Have we in this genealogy, as well as in Matthew's, the line of Joseph? or is this the line of Mary?--a point on which there has been great difference of opinion and much acute discussion. Those who take the former opinion contend that it is the natural sense of this verse, and that no other would have been thought of but for its supposed improbability and the uncertainty which it seems to throw over our Lord's real descent. But it is liable to another difficulty; namely, that in this case Matthew makes Jacob, while Luke makes "Heli," to be Joseph's father; and though the same man had often more than one name, we ought not to resort to that supposition, in such a case as this, without necessity. And then, though the descent of Mary from David would be liable to no real doubt, even though we had no table of her line preserved to us (see, for example, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.2-Luke.1.32">Lu 1:2-32</reference>, and see on <reference osisRef="Luke.2.5">Lu 2:5</reference>), still it does seem unlikely--we say not incredible--that two genealogies of our Lord should be preserved to us, neither of which gives his real descent. Those who take the latter opinion, that we have here the line of Mary, as in Matthew that of Joseph--here His real, there His reputed line--explain the statement about Joseph, that he was "the son of Hell," to mean that he was his son-in-law, as the husband of his daughter Mary (as in <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.11">Ru 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>), and believe that Joseph's name is only introduced instead of Mary's, in conformity with the Jewish custom in such tables. Perhaps this view is attended with fewest difficulties, as it certainly is the best supported. However we decide, it is a satisfaction to know that not a doubt was thrown out by the bitterest of the early enemies of Christianity as to our Lord's real descent from David. On comparing the two genealogies, it will be found that Matthew, writing more immediately for Jews, deemed it enough to show that the Saviour was sprung from Abraham and David; whereas Luke, writing more immediately for Gentiles, traces the descent back to Adam, the parent stock of the whole human family, thus showing Him to be the promised "Seed of the woman." "The possibility of constructing such a table, comprising a period of thousands of years, in an uninterrupted line from father to son, of a family that dwelt for a long time in the utmost retirement, would be inexplicable, had not the members of this line been endowed with a thread by which they could extricate themselves from the many families into which every tribe and branch was again subdivided, and thus hold fast and know the member that was destined to continue the lineage. This thread was the hope that Messiah would be born of the race of Abraham and David. The ardent desire to behold Him and be partakers of His mercy and glory suffered not the attention to be exhausted through a period embracing thousands of years. Thus the member destined to continue the lineage, whenever doubtful, became easily distinguishable, awakening the hope of a final fulfilment, and keeping it alive until it was consummated" [Olshausen]. <div eID="gen27751" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8a9f3f93023790be5c9671c1c5dd2a4551a422d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14322"/><div sID="gen27752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14322"/><hi type="bold">24-30. son of Matthat, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.13-Matt.1.15">Mt 1:13-15</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Luke.3.27">Lu 3:27</reference>, Salathiel is called the son, while in <reference osisRef="Matt.1.12">Mt 1:12</reference>, he is called the father of Zerubbabel. But they are probably different persons. <div eID="gen27752" type="x-p"/>
entries.8de3b4413a3a5bb1967cc9c5338c0991961d3a2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14323"/><div sID="gen27753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14323"/><hi type="bold">38. son of God--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">Ac 17:28</reference>. <chapter eID="Luke.3"/>

entries.3c509c39b1c152a58fd56e44b8e262887896a437: <div eID="gen40058" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen40059" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40060" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40060" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40059" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40061" type="x-p"/> The time in which John the Baptist began to preach, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.1-Luk.3.3">Luk 3:1-3</reference>. The prophecies which were fulfilled in him, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.4-Luk.3.6">Luk 3:4-6</reference>. The matter and success of his preaching, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.7-Luk.3.9">Luk 3:7-9</reference>; among the people, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.10">Luk 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.11">Luk 3:11</reference>; among the publicans, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.12">Luk 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.13">Luk 3:13</reference>; among the soldiers, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.14">Luk 3:14</reference>. His testimony concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.15-Luk.3.18">Luk 3:15-18</reference>. The reason why Herod put him afterwards in prison, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.19">Luk 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.20">Luk 3:20</reference>. He baptizes Christ, on whom the Spirit of God descends, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.21">Luk 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.22">Luk 3:22</reference>. Our Lord's genealogy, vv. 23-38. <div eID="gen40061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen40062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40063" type="x-p"/> Fifteenth year - This was the fifteenth of his principality and thirteenth of his monarchy: for he was two years joint emperor, previously to the death of Augustus. <div eID="gen40063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40064" type="x-p"/> Tiberius Caesar - This emperor succeeded Augustus, in whose reign Christ was born. He began his reign August 19, a.d. 14, reigned twenty-three years, and died March 16, a.d. 37, aged seventy eight years. He was a most infamous character. During the latter part of his reign especially, he did all the mischief he possibly could; and that his tyranny might not end with his life, he chose Caius Caligula for his successor, merely on account of his bad qualities; and of whom he was accustomed to say, This young prince will be a Serpent to the Roman people, and a Phaethon to the rest of mankind. <div eID="gen40064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40065" type="x-p"/> Herod - This was Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who murdered the innocents. It was the same Herod who beheaded John Baptist, and to whom our Lord was sent by Pilate. See the account of the Herod family in the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.2.1">Mat 2:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen40065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40066" type="x-p"/> Iturea and Trachonitis - Two provinces of Syria, on the confines of Judea. <div eID="gen40066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40067" type="x-p"/> Abilene - Another province of Syria, which had its name from Abila, its chief city. <div eID="gen40067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40068" type="x-p"/> These estates were left to Herod Antipas and his brother Philip by the will of their father, Herod the Great; and were confirmed to them by the decree of Augustus. <div eID="gen40068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40069" type="x-p"/> That Philip was tetrarch of Trachonitis, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, we are assured by Josephus, who says that Philip the brother of Herod died in the twentieth year of Tiberius, after he had governed Trachonitis, Batanea, and Gaulonitis thirty-seven years. Antiq. b. xviii. c. 5, s. 6. And Herod continued tetrarch of Galilee till he was removed by Caligula, the successor of Tiberius. Antiq. b. xviii. c. 8, s. 2. <div eID="gen40069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40070" type="x-p"/> That Lysanius was tetrarch of Abilene is also evident from Josephus. He continued in this government till the Emperor Claudius took it from him, a.d. 42, and made a present of it to Agrippa. See Antiq. b. xix. c. 5, s. 1. <div eID="gen40070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40071" type="x-p"/> Tetrarch signifies the ruler of the fourth part of a country. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.1">Mat 14:1</reference>.
entries.77cf95cd94c80ca2677e7be685cc31f8cd46cefe: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen40071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40072" type="x-p"/> Annas and Caiaphas being the high priests - Caiaphas was the son-in-law of Annas or Ananias, and it is supposed that they exercised the high priest's office by turns. It is likely that Annas only was considered as high priest; and that Caiaphas was what the Hebrews termed כהן משנה cohen mishneh, or סגן כהנים sagan cohanim, the high priest's deputy, or ruler of the temple. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.2.4">Mat 2:4</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Joh.18.13">Joh 18:13</reference>. <div eID="gen40072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40073" type="x-p"/> The facts which St. Luke mentions here tend much to confirm the truth of the evangelical history. Christianity differs widely from philosophic system; it is founded in the goodness and authority of God; and attested by historic facts. It differs also from popular tradition, which either has had no pure origin, or which is lost in unknown or fabulous antiquity. It differs also from pagan and Mohammedan revelations, which were fabricated in a corner, and had no witnesses. In the above verses we find the persons, the places, and the times marked with the utmost exactness. It was under the first Caesars that the preaching of the Gospel took place; and in their time, the facts on which the whole of Christianity is founded made their appearance: an age the most enlightened, and best known from the multitude of its historic records. It was in Judea, where every thing that professed to come from God was scrutinized with the most exact and unmerciful criticism. In writing the history of Christianity, the evangelists appeal to certain facts which were publicly transacted in such places, under the government and inspection of such and such persons, and in such particular times. A thousand persons could have confronted the falsehood, had it been one! These appeals are made - a challenge is offered to the Roman government, and to the Jewish rulers and people - a new religion has been introduced in such a place, at such a time - this has been accompanied with such and such facts and miracles! Who can disprove this? All are silent. None appears to offer even an objection. The cause of infidelity and irreligion is at stake! If these facts cannot be disproved, the religion of Christ must triumph. None appears because none could appear. Now let it be observed, that the persons of that time, only, could confute these things had they been false; they never attempted it; therefore these facts are absolute and incontrovertible truths: this conclusion is necessary. Shall a man then give up his faith in such attested facts as these, because, more than a thousand years after, an infidel creeps out, and ventures publicly to sneer at what his iniquitous soul hopes is not true! <div eID="gen40073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40074" type="x-p"/> The word of God came unto John - That is, the Holy Spirit that revealed to him this doctrine of salvation. This came upon him in the desert, where he was living in such a state of austerity as gave him full right to preach all the rigours of penitence to others. Thus we find that the first preachers, historians, and followers of the doctrines of the Gospel were men eminent for the austerity of their lives, the simplicity of their manners, and the sanctity of their conduct; they were authorized by God, and filled with the most precious gifts of his Spirit. And what are the apostles which the new philosophy sends us? Philosophers full of themselves, not guided by the love of truth or wisdom, but ever seeking their own glory; in constant hostility among themselves, because of their separate pretensions to particular discoveries, of the honor of which they would almost as soon lose life as be deprived. Who are they? Men of a mortified life and unblamable conversation? No, they are poets and poetasters; composers of romances, novels, intrigues, farces, comedies, etc., full of extravagance and impurity. They are pretended moralists that preach up pleasure and sensual gratification, and dissolve, as far as they can, the sacred and civil ties that unite and support society. They are men whose guilt is heightened by their assuming the sacred name of philosophers, and dignifying their impure system with a name at which Philosophy herself blushes and bleeds.

entries.e59f85aba7075ad3b425018dcd4d97039a9cb7ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen40078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40079" type="x-p"/> What shall we do then? - The preaching of the Baptist had been accompanied with an uncommon effusion of that Spirit which convinces of sin, righteousness, and judgment.
